exam: A 25‑year‑old woman presents with fever, splenomegaly and pancytopenia. What is the next best investigation? — Peripheral smear to look for malaria parasites or schistocytes; if negative, consider aplastic anemia or hypersplenism.

A patient with sickle cell disease develops sudden abdominal pain and a drop in Hb. What is the likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Splenic sequestration; urgent splenectomy or transfusion if haemodynamic instability.
A child has pallor, fatigue and a low Hb of 8 g/dL. Ferritin is 30 ng/mL. What is the most likely cause and first treatment? — Iron deficiency; start oral ferrous sulfate and dietary advice.

A 60‑year‑old man with HIV presents with fever and thrombocytopenia (platelets 25×10^9/L). What is the first step in management? — Start broad‑spectrum antibiotics for possible sepsis and consider platelet transfusion if bleeding.
A patient with a history of malaria presents with jaundice and a high reticulocyte count. What is the likely mechanism? — Hemolytic anaemia due to parasite‑induced red cell destruction.

A 30‑year‑old man has a normal Hb but a WBC of 2×10^9/L. What is the most likely cause and next test? — Neutropenia; check for viral infections (EBV, CMV) and consider bone marrow aspirate if persistent.

A patient with a known hemoglobinopathy presents with sudden drop in Hb and abdominal pain. What complication should you suspect and how to confirm? — Splenic sequestration; confirm with ultrasound showing enlarged spleen and rapid drop in Hb.
A 45‑year‑old woman with chronic fatigue has a platelet count of 50×10^9/L. What is the most common reversible cause in this setting? — Iron deficiency; treat with iron and repeat count.
ai.title: Blood Cell Disorders
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Blood cells are central to oxygen transport, immunity and clotting. In low‑resource settings, infections, nutritional deficiencies and hemoglobinopathies dominate. Rapid bedside assessment and simple tests guide urgent care.

sections.p: Blood cells—erythrocytes, leukocytes and platelets—perform oxygen delivery, immune defense and haemostasis. Their morphology and count are altered by infections, nutritional deficiencies, genetic disorders and malignancy.

Clinical reasoning starts with the patient’s history, signs and simple investigations. In resource‑limited settings, the peripheral smear, full blood count (FBC) and basic chemistry are often the only data available.

b: Sickle cell: vaso‑occlusive crises, splenic sequestration
sections.p: Common causes in East Africa include malaria, HIV, TB, schistosomiasis, nutritional deficiencies (iron, folate, B12) and sickle cell disease. Prompt recognition prevents complications such as severe anaemia, sepsis and bleeding.
